content: Electrocardiograph (EKG) artifacts are abnormalities observed on an EKG tracing that do not originate from the electrical activity of the heart. These artifacts can distort the normal components of the EKG, such as the P wave, QRS complex, T wave, and PR or ST segments. Recognizing these artifacts is crucial to avoid unnecessary diagnostic tests or therapeutic interventions. Causes of EKG Artifacts Internal Causes Internal causes of EKG artifacts are physiological in nature and often result from the patient’s own movements or muscular activity: Patient motion: Movements such as large body swings or epidermal stretching can interfere with electronic filtration, leading to significant distortions. Tremors and shivering are common sources of motion artifacts. Even simple activities like brushing or combing hair during ambulatory EKG monitoring can produce disturbances. Muscular activity: Muscle contractions can generate small spikes on the EKG, which are filtered electronically but may still appear as artifacts. External Causes External causes are non-physiological and often involve interference from electrical devices or issues with the EKG equipment: Electromagnetic interference: This can arise from power line disturbances, light fixtures, electrocautery devices, or radiofrequency-emitting devices like mobile phones. Cable and electrode issues: Problems such as insufficient electrode gel, misplaced leads, inappropriate filter settings, broken wires, loose connections, or static energy accumulation can lead to artifacts. Medical equipment: Devices used in operating rooms or intensive care units, such as amplifiers, filters, or electrodes, can interfere with EKG monitoring. Identification of EKG Artifacts Artifacts can distort one or more components of the EKG tracing. While they are often easily identifiable and do not follow a specific pattern, it is essential to distinguish them from genuine cardiac abnormalities to prevent misdiagnosis. For example, artifacts affecting the ST segment may mimic ST segment depression or elevation, which could be misinterpreted as myocardial ischemia or infarction. Differentiating Artifacts from Ventricular Tachycardia Artifacts can sometimes resemble arrhythmias like ventricular tachycardia or atrial flutter. Misdiagnosis in such cases can lead to inappropriate treatments. Key features that help differentiate artifacts from true ventricular tachycardia include: The absence of hemodynamic instability during the event. Normal QRS complexes interspersed within the artifact. An unstable baseline before, after, or during the event. Association of the artifact with bodily movement. Huang et al. described three specific signs to distinguish tremor-induced pseudo-ventricular tachycardia from true ventricular tachycardia: 1. Sinus sign: One of the frontal leads (I, II, or III) may show a normal sinus rhythm with intact P, QRS, and T waves, as one upper limb may be free of tremor. 2. Spike sign: Tiny, regular or irregular spikes may appear among wide-QRS complexes. 3. Notch sign: Notches superimposed on the wide-QRS-like artifact, corresponding to the sinus rhythm cycle length. Electrode Misplacement Misplaced electrodes are a common source of artifacts that can mimic life-threatening arrhythmias. Early recognition and correction of electrode placement are essential to avoid unnecessary interventions. The REVERSE mnemonic has been proposed as a systematic approach to identifying and addressing EKG artifacts. Other Common Artifacts Electrodes on the torso: Placing electrodes on the torso instead of the limbs can alter the electrical vectors, producing pseudo-Q waves or pseudo-ST segment elevation that may mimic myocardial infarction. Telemetry interference: Overlapping telemetry and EKG electrodes can cause electromagnetic interference, leading to ST segment deviations. Loose wires: A straight line may resemble asystole, while a wavy line may mimic fibrillation, but these artifacts are usually limited to one or two leads. Tall T waves: A tall T wave may be mistaken for an R wave, resulting in an erroneously high digital heart rate. Lead placement issues: Misplaced leads can obscure P waves, creating the appearance of a heart block. Motion artifacts: Movements such as chest percussion or physiotherapy can mimic ventricular fibrillation. Consequences of EKG Artifacts Artifacts can compromise the quality of the EKG and, more importantly, mimic genuine cardiac abnormalities. If not recognized, they may lead to unnecessary diagnostic tests, invasive procedures, or inappropriate treatments, such as the administration of antiarrhythmic medications. Correction of EKG Artifacts To minimize artifacts, attention should be given to proper electrode placement and lead connections. High-quality, well-maintained EKG equipment can reduce the impact of routine electrical or motion-related disturbances, though complete elimination of artifacts is not always possible. Physicians must remain vigilant and consider artifacts in their differential diagnosis when interpreting EKGs. Examples of EKG Artifacts Artifacts can arise from various sources, including patient movement, tremors, or electrical interference. Examples include: Movement artifacts: Increasing movement artifacts in patients with Parkinson’s disease. Baseline drift: Often seen after lead connection or following electrical cardioversion, as the EKG amplifier adjusts to find the baseline. Electrical interference: Background distortion from fluorescent lights or other electrical appliances can mimic atrial fibrillation. Loose wires: These can produce straight or wavy lines that resemble asystole or fibrillation, respectively. Tall T waves: These may be misinterpreted as R waves, leading to an overestimation of heart rate.
